summary: Before landing: one reader meets the map cold as a person would; one sets what changed this morning against what it stands on. Read only.

cold.after_two_minutes:
One idea and one impression.

The idea: anything that picks by a score (a reward, a judge, a market) can eat up what the score leaves out, can entrench itself once the score is refitted from its own choices (the keyboard example made that land), and can end with nobody left who would have noticed (the survey answered only by those who stayed). There is one escape the authors say follows from the process itself and several that need something added.

The impression: a sheet of rows and boxes with a numbered, coloured route through it, each line drawn by how well it is known, written by an AI that is careful about what is proved. The line "Close to what others call: Goodhart's law; the Matthew effect; regulatory capture" told me what I was looking at faster than the opening paragraph did.

What I did not have yet: what the rows are (so what the map is a map of), what "the course itself" and "given from outside" mean, who "the rest" are, what "read the loss" means, and why a page whose first path is about scoring rules opens with "how anything forms, lasts, changes and ends". The third sentence of the opening ("the loss gets back to the rule in time, the rest count it, and the judgments together go against what the rule favoured at two updates running") I read twice and passed over.
cold.after_fifteen_minutes:
The shape: one sheet, five bands (what a thing lives on; what a choosing goes by; a view and how things are; between things that keep going; anything that keeps going), 14 rows that each ask a question, 50 boxes that are possible answers, 105 arrows whose line style says how each is known. Five told paths and seven tests are laid on that same sheet. That it is one map and not a set is true of what I was shown.

The first path: I can retell it from its five group headings (how it closes, another way in, the ways out, where it is too late, what no law shows) and from "What this path shows", which sorts the steps by how they are known. The lock is proved. That the loss keeps growing is assumed. That those who would notice are removed is shown only in constructed examples. One way out follows from the process and four need something added. How it starts is in no law. "What the work wants" is the clearest paragraph on the page, and "This is wanted; it is not shown" is the sentence I would quote to someone else.

The tests: the most readable part. Each is told as situation / what the reasoning said / what was seen / what was taken as which box / what gave way / what else would give the same. In five of seven something gave way, and nearly always it was the "pairing" (how the case was matched to the boxes), not a theorem. This is where reasoning and situation are visibly kept apart and their meeting shown. I understood that distinction from the tests, not from the legend.

What I still do not have:
(a) The model the proofs are about. The steps speak of "the same side", "that side's share", "the lead", "the rest", "what sets the rule", "the shapers", "the judging of the rule", and nowhere is the cast set out once.
(b) What an arrow between boxes in different rows means, when a thing is said to stand in one box of every row at once.
(c) Whether any person has checked any of it: "How far it goes" describes AI readers checking AI wordings.
(d) What "the theory of becoming" is, and how the four other bands bear on the first path beyond sharing a sheet.
(e) What "Place something you know" does; no picture of it was among those sent. Nor did I see the static SVGs the Markdown pages embed; my remarks on the picture are from the screenshots of the interactive page.
cold.where_i_would_stop:
Three places, in order.

1. The first pull to leave is step 3 of the first path (/Users/ren/theories/tmp/r7/sheet/v2/out/THE-MAP.md line 31): three sentences about what is "given, not derived", written for someone checking the proof, just where the story has started to move. A casual visitor leaves here. I skimmed it and went on because step 4 has the survey example.

2. I stopped reading step by step at step 8 ("Together, those that set the rule can tell it only if at least one of them can"). From there I read only the bold headings and the tags, then jumped to "What this path shows" and "What the work wants". The ways out, steps 8 to 13, are the payoff of the path and are the part with no example at all.

3. I would stop for good in "How far it goes", at the second sentence of its long paragraph (line 130): one block of about 300 words accounting for which AI reader set which wording against what. By then I have had the tests and the whole map, and nothing after it promises anything new.

On the interactive page I would instead click "What each turn brings back" (microphone, shower tap, interest on interest: the friendliest path, most steps carry an example) and one test, "Three AI fishers". In PATHS.md I read that test in full and stopped inside "Small trained policies" at "entry check" and "policy gradient". PLACES.md I would only ever look things up in. As a look-up page it works (each box: what it is, an example, what leads out, what leads in, tests laid there) until the fold-outs "Dynamics of the atlas placed here" and the Lean names, which are for insiders.
cold.is_it_a_map:
For a chosen path, mostly yes: the picture itself shows what happens. In k-lock.png I can follow the numbers without the side text: "Follows its own picks, not yet locked" to "Holds itself in place" to "Using up what is not counted" to "What would read the loss is gone" to "Judged only by its own picks", with green lines leaving toward the green-dashed boxes and violet ones toward "Gets back, but the lock stays", "Past turning back" and "Ended". The box names are states said in a few words, so a route through them reads as a course of events. That is a map of what happens, not a filing plan. k-returns.png shows the form at its best: two rows, one box fanning out to five outcomes, fourteen numbered moves, nothing crossing.

What the picture does not show, and only the words beside it do:
- What makes each move happen. Lit arrows carry a number and nothing else. Short tags exist ("every update favours the same side", "nothing left counts the loss", "the rest count the loss, and outweigh"), and the test overlay prints such labels on the sheet, but the path overlay does not.
- How well each link is known, at reading size. Solid, dashed and dotted are hard to tell apart once the group colour is on them. The red route 1 to 6 looks like one mechanism, though link 3 is assumed and link 4 comes from constructed examples only.
- What the four colours mean (red closing, green ways out, violet too late, grey no law). It is in no legend; I worked it out from the coloured dashes beside the group headings.
- The hub. Around "Holds itself in place" and "Using up what is not counted" about eight lines meet. Badges 2 and 13 sit on each other, 3 and 14 are side by side, and the long double lines for "one is a case of the other" (steps 1 and 6) run down two bands and cross 14 and 15.

The whole sheet (k-whole.png) shows the shape and where arrows are thick, and the last band reads well alone. But 105 unlabelled lines are not readable as a whole. In "A view and how things are" a dozen arcs loop over and under a single row and I cannot tell where any lands; between "What is taken against what comes back" and "What lives on it" the lines tangle. As a whole it is an index to click, not a picture to read.

The test overlay (k-season.png, k-season-zoom.png) does show reasoning meeting situation on the sheet: where a thing was set up, where it was found instead, and the arrow the reasoning went by. But the marks need a key (a crossed circle, dashed-outline numbers). The labels "4. 4.45 against 3.57; unresolved" and "1. nearly emptied, both kinds" stack on one box corner with four badges, and a dashed line runs through the name of "Gets back to the rule in time".

One thing the picture leaves unclear in itself: arrows along a row are changes of state; arrows between rows link answers to different questions about the same thing. Both are drawn the same.

Chinese side (k-zh.png): the same sheet, properly bilingual. Two small faults: the off-sheet pointer at the right edge is clipped ("→ 换了一茬，格局…"), and a violet test dot sits on the first character of 跟着结果改，还没定住 (in English too).

seven_complaints.complaint: (1) Hard for a human to read
seven_complaints.evidence: The layout is now easy to move through: lead, picture, legend, a path under five plain headings, tests, whole map. The sentences are not. They are theorem statements in plain words: all the conditions, then the conclusion. Step 2: "if every update favours the same side, and no less when that side's share is larger, the rule is locked in from the step after its second update, wherever it started". Step 15: "no rule that goes only by whether those things keep going can read it in time". Step 8: "Together, those that set the rule can tell it only if at least one of them can". The opening paragraph's second sentence is about fifty words with three claims. What I understood at once were the three steps with a "Such as" (2 keyboard, 4 survey, 7 lobbying); three more carry a test note; twelve of eighteen have nothing concrete. The other paths are easier ("What each turn brings back" has an example on most steps), so the hardest path is the one met first. The Chinese side reads the same way: the box names are livelier than the English (用掉的不在账上, 留着不如拿走, 查错的也在圈里), the step sentences as heavy.

seven_complaints.complaint: (2) No real map of the dynamics
seven_complaints.evidence: Answered for a path: boxes are states, arrows are moves, a numbered route reads as a course of events (k-lock.png, k-returns.png), and tests are laid on the same sheet (k-season.png). It still holds in three ways. What makes each move happen is not on the picture, only beside it. The whole sheet (k-whole.png) is 105 unlabelled lines, unreadable in the band "A view and how things are" and between the second and third rows of "What it lives on". And nothing on the sheet says what in-row and cross-row arrows each mean, though the side panel says a thing stands in one box of every row at once.

THE-MAP.md is about 3,500 words, PATHS.md 13,000, PLACES.md 17,000 (one read-only word count; no file was changed). On the first page the first path is told four times: the opening paragraph, the 18 steps, "What this path shows", "What the work wants". Step 9's condition is given in full three times (lead, step 9, "What the work wants"). "Given from outside" comes about a dozen times on the page. "How far it goes" has one 300-word paragraph. The interactive page folds each step's detail under "In full", which is the right move; the Markdown page has no fold, and steps 3 and 15 carry their full caveats in the telling.

seven_complaints.complaint: (4) Too much AI vocabulary and vocabulary of its own
seven_complaints.evidence: The AI and theory vocabulary is nearly gone from the front page: one "meta-attractor" (step 6), "the Lean", the test codes (IN1, LA2, MQ3, LA4 (Stage A), EM1, LA1b, TR7A), and in the tests "policies", "learning rule", "control". What has taken its place is a private dialect of ordinary words used as fixed terms, harder to spot because nothing marks them as terms: "the course", "given from outside", "built example", "the rest", "the lead", "read the loss", "laid on", "the pairing", "gave way", "the account", "no law drawn", "ties". "Read" alone carries four senses on one page: to register a loss; a "reading" that is not proved; an "AI reader" who checks; "this judge does not read as a pool of readers counted by kind". None is linked to the Glossary the nav bar names. Deeper in, the insiders' words return whole: "policy gradient", "entry check", "is a profile with restraint an equilibrium?" (PATHS.md tests), and the PLACES.md fold-outs ("Selection blind beyond the coupling closure").

seven_complaints.complaint: (5) Readings unstructured; wants layers, an index, entry points, something like a Wikipedia
seven_complaints.evidence: Mostly answered. There are layers: a lead, a path, the other paths with step counts, tests in two sentences each with a page behind, an index of every box by row, and PLACES.md, which is the Wikipedia-like part: one entry per box with a definition, an example, kin in other traditions, "From here", "Into here", tests laid there. The interactive page's chips (paths, tests, "Place something you know", the whole map, English/中文) are real entry points. What still holds: the Markdown page opens with a bar of twenty links before a word of content, four of them other map-like pages (Atlas, Graph, Connections, "Where everything is"), so "one map" is true of the sheet and not of the door. There is no way in from what a newcomer already knows: the 45 names such as Goodhart's law or the tragedy of the commons sit under paths and boxes but are not an index. Nothing marks which part is the two-minute read and which the hour. The page's own terms have no key on the page.

The words avoid good and bad, and the page says so twice ("an order of open and closed, not of better and worse"; "This is wanted; it is not shown"). The picture and the frame say otherwise. Red is used for "How it closes", green for "The ways out" and for the outline of the three wanted boxes, violet for "Where it is too late". The wanted boxes sit in the left half of their rows and the ends ("Ended", "Past turning back", "Even the checks are its own", "Each waits for the other", "Sees it, lacks the means") at the right, so in four of five bands left-to-right reads as well-to-doomed whatever the caption says. The first path's model is two-sided in its own terms: "the same side" against "the rest", "the shapers" against "the rest". And every arrow is sorted by one binary, "of the course itself" or "given from outside". As a newcomer I did not mind the predicament-and-exits shape; it is what makes the first path a story. But it is a valued shape, and the disclaimer does not undo what colour and layout show.

Mostly answered: the candour is the most serious thing here. Every step carries how it is known; the tests report what failed ("63% of stretches fell, where the reasoning said all would"; "no law was tested"; "What else would give the same"); the aim is marked as a want. What still undercuts it: the opening scope ("how anything forms, lasts, changes and ends") against tests that are three AI fishers and an apple patch, five runs at a time; the heading "Where the reasoning met the world" over seven tests of which six are built games; "How far it goes", which read cold says AI readers corrected "most" of AI wordings and that later changes "have not been set against the Lean again", with no word on what a person has read; names from Laozi, Mencius, Epicurus, the Gītā and Whitehead set beside shower taps without saying which step each is close to; internal codes; and unpolished generated text deeper in. That last: doubled full stops and a capital after a colon in the test rows of PATHS.md (lines 431-435, 460-464, 489-493); "?." in PLACES.md (lines 22, 169, 443, 503); a Lean name in Chinese with no gloss (PLACES.md line 168); and in "Giving that waits on giving" step 7 lists the same arrow and tag as step 6 (PATHS.md lines 242, 244) though its sentence is about a different law.

own_vocabulary: "the course", "proved of the course itself": opening paragraph (THE-MAP.md line 11), 'What this path shows', whole-map caption (line 93). Never defined. I guessed: the process as it runs, with nothing added.

"given from outside", "proved only with something given from outside": legend, steps 3, 10-13, 17, about a dozen times on the page. It means two different things: a premise the theorem assumes (step 3) and an arrangement someone must supply (steps 10-13).
"given, not derived": step 3.
"built example", "built case": opening paragraph, legend, steps 4 and 16. I guessed: a constructed toy model.
"read the loss", "readers of the loss", "counters of the loss", "what would read the loss": opening paragraph, steps 4 and 16, a box name.

"reading" in three further senses: 'a reading, not proved' (step 18, legend); 'AI reader', 'one reader so far' ('How far it goes'; PLACES.md tags); 'does not read as a pool of readers counted by kind' (test LA2 summary).
"the rest", "the rest count it": opening paragraph, steps 9 and 14, the box 'The rest count too'. The rest of what is never said.
"the same side", "that side's share", "the lead", "a lock which goes by the lead alone": steps 2, 3, 5, 16. 'The lead' first appears in step 3 with no introduction.
"the shapers", "shaping the rule": steps 7 and 11, a row name.
"what sets the rule", "the judging of the rule", "judgments taken together": steps 6, 8, 9, 14.
"meta-attractor", "its closed form": step 6.
"the account": step 6; 'the account's 183 dynamics' ('How far it goes'); 'the account's own view' (tests in PATHS.md).
"law", "no law drawn", "the laws take...": throughout. That it means a machine-checked theorem on a stated model is said only at line 128.
"Lean", "the Lean", "no anchor in the Lean yet", "tied to a definition or a law in the Lean": 'What the work wants'; 'How far it goes'.
"laid on", "a test is laid on it": legend, step notes, tests heading.
"the pairing", "gave way", "taken as": tests section. A good term once one test has been read in full; it needs one line of introduction.
"best by the rule", "with room to gain", "the spare", "lowest allowed level": steps 13 and 15.
"every best course", "best reply": 'Living on what comes back' steps 5 and 12; PLACES.md.
"tie", "the one web", "whatever its ties": whole-map caption (line 93); side panel 'THE ONE WEB' in k-whole.png ('Each row of the first four bands reads a tie of one web').

"dynamics" as a counted noun, "Dynamics of the atlas placed here": 'How far it goes'; PLACES.md fold-outs, whose entries are insiders' titles ('Readings carried along a line, told apart by its standing late only within its coupling closure').
"stretches" (test MQ3); "control", "entry check", "policies", "learning rule", "policy gradient", "seeds", "frozen settings" (LA4 and later tests in PATHS.md).
Test codes IN1, LA2, MQ3, LA4 (Stage A), EM1, LA1b, TR7A, and LA1c in passing: tests list and PATHS.md.
"a difference sent out", "mark", "gap", "band": 'What each turn brings back', intro and steps 5, 11, 12.
"one order further": step 18.
Untranslated: 'Laozi 77: 損有餘而補不足' under 'What each turn brings back', where the Mencius and Guoyu quotes beside it get an English gloss.
says_more_than_shown: The opening, 'A map of how anything forms, lasts, changes and ends' (THE-MAP.md line 11). What is drawn is five paths and 50 boxes; forming has hardly a box; line 130 says most of the account's recorded passages and 59 of its 66 tests are not on the map.

The heading 'Where the reasoning met the world' (line 77). Six of the seven tests are built games played by AI models or small learners. In four the entry itself says no law was tested or on trial. The one with field data (113 fish stocks) is where a condition of the reasoning failed. The entries are candid; the heading is not.

'Solid where it is proved' and 'Unmarked steps are proved' (lines 15, 25). Proved of a stated model, which is said only at line 128. Making 'proved' the unmarked default also lends the everyday examples (keyboard, lobbying) a theorem's weight, though line 130 says the examples are illustrations.

The red route 'How it closes', steps 1 to 6, reads and is drawn as one mechanism. By the page's own summary link 3 is assumed and link 4 comes from constructed examples. So the lock is proved, but that a lock uses anything up, or removes whoever would notice, is not derived from it. The text says this; the heading and the picture do not.

Step 9 says the rule 'turns for good'; step 16 says that after it had turned 'the lock came back for good'. Read together, either step 9 claims more than it shows or the two contradict. The condition that separates them (the ones counting the loss are still there) is not stated at step 9.

Step 6's test note, 'locked in 5 of 5 runs where nothing read the loss', sits under the step that names the meta-attractor. It is five runs of a judge that began under a starting rule favouring lists, and the same test's page says the pairing gave way and the scoring rule passed a course that was not locked. The note at step 14 carries its caveat; this one does not.

'Close to what others call' (Goodhart, the Matthew effect, regulatory capture, Sen, Collingridge; on other paths Laozi, Mencius, Epicurus, the Gītā, Whitehead, Micaiah). Set beside a path, the list reads as a claim to cover them. Which step is close to which is not shown on the path, and the disclaimer ('it is not the source's agreement') is at line 130.

The whole-map caption (line 93): 'most that run right are proved of the course itself; most that run back need something given from outside'. It reads as a finding about the world (things close by themselves and open only with help). It is a count over arrows 'drawn so far', on a left-to-right order the page says 'is ours'. The qualifiers are there; the sentence weighs more than they carry.
'What the work wants' says four arrows lead into 'The cost counts'. The path picture beside it shows two (9 and 10); the other two are only on the whole map.

PATHS.md, 'Giving that waits on giving', step 7 (line 244): the arrow listed under it is step 6's, with step 6's tag ('each can do without the one that lapsed'), so what the step says is not what is shown beneath it.

changes.what: Give every step of the first path a case, and carry one case through it. The boxes already hold a matching family: a catch quota met every year while the seabed wears away (step 1), residents downstream now on the board (step 8), a quota set from the seabed as well (step 9), a trial that counts every patient enrolled (step 12), a minority report outvoted every year (step 14). Add one AI case, such as a ranking model retrained on what it ranked first, since the lead names a training run.
changes.where: THE-MAP.md and PATHS.md, first path, steps 1, 3, 5, 6, 8 to 16. The examples are in PLACES.md at boxes b2-uncounted, b2-felt, b2-counted, b3-list, b2-heard, b3-rest.

In the same place say what 'the course', 'given from outside', 'built example', 'law' and 'read' mean on this page, and that 'given from outside' covers two things: a premise a theorem assumes (step 3) and something that has to be supplied (steps 10 to 13).
changes.where: THE-MAP.md between line 25 and 'How it closes'; the same in the interactive side panel above step 1.

changes.what: Rewrite the opening paragraph as four short sentences with the scope the page has, and bring the meaning of 'proved' up into 'How to read it'. Say what is drawn so far (five paths, fifty boxes) beside 'how anything forms, lasts, changes and ends'; drop 'at two updates running' from the lead; replace 'solid where it is proved' with 'solid where it is proved of a stated model, checked by machine; whether a real case fits is what the tests show'.
changes.where: THE-MAP.md lines 11 and 15, and the same lead on the interactive page. The sentences to move up are the first two of 'How far it goes' (line 128).
changes.why: This is all a two-minute reader takes. As it stands they take 'anything' and 'proved' unqualified, and the qualification is more than a hundred lines below.

changes.what: Tell steps 3, 8 and 15 in one plain sentence each and move the proof-checker's caveats under a fold (the interactive page has 'In full'; give the Markdown a details block). Step 3 could be: 'The lock does not notice the loss: it runs the same however much is used up. That the loss goes on growing is assumed, not proved.' In the same pass settle 'for good': add to step 9 the condition it holds under (while those counting the loss are still there), so it no longer collides with step 16.

Either state it plainly as the work's want (the three green boxes) and keep it to that one mark, or take it out of the rest: use hues for the step groups that do not read as stop and go, and keep line style for how a thing is known. edits.where: item 3: lead_en, its last two sentences
edits.old: One way out is proved of the course itself: the loss gets back to the rule in time, the rest count it, and the judgments together go against what the rule favoured at two updates running. Every other way out drawn needs something given from outside.
edits.new: One way out is a law of the course itself, under its condition: where the loss gets back to the rule in time, the rest count it, and the judgments together go against what the rule favoured at two updates running, the rule turns for good. No law drawn says what brings a loss to get back to the rule or to be counted. Every other way out drawn needs something given from outside, or is shown only in a built example or as a reading.
edits.why: (a) What is proved is a conditional (step 9; arrow b2.felt to b2.counted: 'Where the rest count the loss and judgments taken together go against what the rule favoured ... the rule turns for good if, and only if, they still go against it at the next update'). The paragraph listed the three conditions after 'is proved ...:' with no 'where' and no consequent, so their happening read as proved. (b) The path's own shows line adds 'No law drawn says what makes a loss reach what sets the rule, or come to be counted'; the only arrows into 'Gets back to the rule in time' are two boundaries and a reading. Without it 'of the course itself' reads as a way out the course takes by itself. (c) 'Every other way out drawn needs something given from outside' was tidier than the map: there are also the built case under step 10 (named in the shows line), the built arrow from 'Holds itself in place' back to 'Follows its own picks, not yet locked', and the reading from 'What would read the loss is gone' to 'Gets back to the rule in time'.
